_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 1 Mathematics unit lecture film, Shapes and Sizes. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow the lesson opener's three lecture parts (flat and solid shapes; sides, corners and faces; comparing size) opened out into six teaching chapters, in the lesson page's own examples: its flat shapes (circle, triangle, square: step 4 'Flat shapes'), its solids (cube like a dice, sphere like a ball, cylinder like a tin, cone with a point: steps 6 and 14), its one sorting question (step 7 'Flat or solid?'), its three ribbons short-longer-longest (step 9), its melon and strawberry on the balance (step 10, question 1) and its full and empty jugs (step 11).
title: Shapes and Sizes
subtitle: Grade 1 Mathematics
objectives: Identify, describe and sort 2D shapes by their characteristics or properties, including reference to number of sides and whether the sides are curved or straight.
Identify, describe and sort 3D shapes by their properties, including reference to the number of faces, edges and whether faces are flat or curved.
Use familiar language to describe length, including long, longer, longest, thin, thinner, thinnest, short, shorter, shortest, tall, taller and tallest.
Use familiar language to describe mass, including heavy, light, less and more.
Use familiar language to describe capacity, including full, empty, less and more.

beats.say: Shapes are all around you. Some are flat. Some are solid.
You can also compare their sizes. Longer, heavier, holds more.
A flat shape lies on the page. You could draw it yourself.
Here is a square. Count its sides: one, two, three, four.
Four sides. Now the corners, where two sides meet.
One, two, three, four. A square has four corners too.
A triangle has three sides and three corners.
A circle is different. Its edge curves right round, with no corners.
A solid shape is not flat. You can hold it in your hand.
A cube is like a dice. Its flat surfaces are called faces.
Count them: one, two, three, four, five, six faces.
An edge is where two faces meet. A cube has twelve edges.
A sphere is like a ball. One curved face, no edges.
A cylinder is like a tin. A cone has a point on top.
How do you tell a flat shape from a solid one?
Ask one question. Could I pick it up and turn it over?
A circle is drawn on paper, so it is flat. A ball you can hold.
A square is flat. A cube is solid, made of six square faces.
Here are three ribbons, all of different lengths.
Line up one end, so they all start together.
Now see which one goes further. This one is short.
This one is longer. And this one is the longest of all.
Which one is heavier? A balance can tell you.
Put a melon in one pan and a strawberry in the other.
The side that goes down holds the heavier thing.
The melon side goes down. So the melon is heavier.
Capacity means how much a container can hold.

at.hold: how much a container can hold

beats.say: This jug is full. The water is right up to the top.
This one is empty. It has none at all.
In between, the jug where the water is higher holds more.
Flat shapes have sides and corners. Solid shapes have faces and edges.
A flat shape you draw. A solid shape you can hold.
Longer, heavier, holds more: you can compare any two things.
Now go and hunt for shapes at home.
